source.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
source.authors: Yi-Fan Luo; Zhen-Nan Zhou; Mei Wang; Bin Dong

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether safety behaviour can be disrupted by changing a restricted set of MLP neuron activations, using an inference-time reweighting intervention rather than the claim’s fine-tuning or token-distribution measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports HarmBench attack success rates for its MLP reweighting attacks and measurements of how many neuron factors were changed. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefill, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes, or deepening safety. Results for other jailbreak methods in Table 1 are comparisons, not rows for this claim.
record.test_reason: An inference-time attack scales MLP neuron activations at the end-of-prompt template positions. It reports HarmBench ASR together with how few factors change. This bears on V5: whether a small, localized set of components carries safety. It is a different method from weight pruning or rank removal but aims at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that reweighting MLP neurons at end-of-sentence inferences substantially compromises safety. They hypothesize that harmfulness assessment happens there, and leave the precise mechanism open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses inference-time scaling of MLP neuron activations at selected prompt-ending positions, optimized to elicit affirmative continuations; it is not fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, or compliant-prefix prefill.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and attack setup: prompt-specific and prompt-general methods have different reported ASRs, and the authors report weaker prompt-general performance on Gemma models. Factor sparsity also varies with regularization and stopping condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-relevant computation sits at the fixed end-of-prompt template tokens (e.g. 'assistant', '<|end_header_id|>'). Modifying only those positions, and leaving response-generating inferences untouched, suffices to jailbreak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal decisions are anchored in the chat-template positions before the response, not only in the first response tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: preprint; under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2025
record.problems: The attack objective and positive prefixes are heuristic-driven, as the authors acknowledge. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASRs. The paper states that the mechanism’s precise role remains unresolved; the activation reweighting intervention does not establish that permanent weights or ranks alone carry safety.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 results for GCG, AP, ORTHO, GCG-M, Human, and Direct Request are comparison methods rather than the study’s MLP reweighting intervention. Standard-task scores in Table 2 and hidden-state cosine similarities in Figure 3 do not measure the versions tested here.

untested.parts: Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefill, suffixes and decoding changes. Response-generating positions are explicitly left unmodified.
Permanent weight or rank edits. Sparsity is reported only for LLaMA-3 8B prompt-general, not for other models or the prompt-specific method.

missing.what: ASR of the prompt-general method across L1 penalty values rho; it stays effective even with rho near 0.

Capability preservation after prompt-general reweighting. Benchmark scores are mostly within ~1–2 points; Gemma-2 2B ARC drops 9.6. This is relevant to V5's claim that safety can be removed while capabilities are kept.

record.verdict_notes: The record omits the Direct Request column, which is the natural baseline; ASR rows should carry it. The study is not an original source. The intervention scales activations per position and does not edit weights, so its bearing on V5's 'weights or ranks' wording is by analogy to neuron-level localization. The sparsity figures are for LLaMA-3 8B only.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilling compliant tokens, suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
The study reweights MLP neuron activations during inference; it does not edit model weights or ranks directly, nor establish that a small set of permanent parameters alone carries safety behaviour.
Whether training data or the training objective produces shallow safety.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and whether that safety holds up.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-3 8B/70B, Qwen-2 7B/72B, Yi-1.5 6B (prompt-specific and prompt-general), and Gemma-2 2B prompt-specific
relationships.reason: Small activation rescaling at a few template positions raises ASR from DR baselines of 0–34 to 77–97 (R1–R8, R11). LLaMA-3 8B sparsity measures show <3% of factors below 0.9 and ~2% average modulation (R12, R13).

source_check.notes: Read=full: PDF pages 3, 7, 8, 14, 15, 16 inspected and match the supplied text; Table 1 is cleanly laid out; no version mismatch seen. Accepted objections: R13 condition (n); R14 condition (n, omits T(n-2)/L13); R14 baseline (n, text gives 3% main-setting comparator, though measured at different position T(n-1) L18); V5.against[12] partly (wording stronger than 'somewhat inferior'). Rejected: none, except the l0 DR-range remark, which was dropped as a muddled flaw (label unchanged). Fig 2(b) y-axis resized and Fig 8(b) clipped at 50, so the 3% and 0.1% shares are text-stated only. Baseline is stored as not stated on 12 rows where Table 1 DR gives one. Prompt-specific was run only on 2B-7B models.

statements.correction: Table 1: DR 2.5, prompt-general 94.3 (ORTHO 94.3). Fig 2(b): under 3% of factors below 0.9 at T(n-1), L18; about 2% average modulation at the most modified factors.
statements.problem: Numbers are right for this study: 2.5 to 94.3 for LLaMA-3 8B prompt-general, under 3% below 0.9 at L18, T(n-1), greedy decoding, LLaMA-Guard-3, 159 HarmBench behaviors. The 2.5 is the Direct Request column, not an attack baseline.

statements.correction: Appendix D: rho=1e-3 until convergence, ASR about 87%, below 0.1% of factors under 0.9, quality somewhat inferior (occasional incoherence, overly brief responses).
statements.problem: Wording 'degraded or incoherent responses' is stronger than the text: ASR is still about 87% and quality is 'somewhat inferior', with occasional incoherence and overly brief answers. Section 4.4 says early-stopped large-rho runs behave differently.

statements.correction: Table 1: Gemma-2 2B prompt-general 78.0 vs prompt-specific 94.3; Gemma-2 27B prompt-general 67.3, no prompt-specific run. ORTHO 91.2 (2B), 74.1 (27B). Authors say the cause is unclear and suspect more complex safety mechanisms.
statements.problem: Gemma prompt-general is weaker than other models and than ORTHO on Gemma. But prompt-specific was run only on 2B-7B models, so no prompt-specific result exists for Gemma-2 27B. The comparison holds for 2B only (78.0 vs 94.3).

statements.correction: Appendix D: ASR about 87% at rho=1e-3 with occasional incoherent and overly brief responses. Table 2: capability about unchanged except Gemma-2 2B.
statements.problem: Consistent with R14/R15: the sparse converged solution showed somewhat inferior coherence. The authors do not frame it as a separability point. Capability elsewhere is mostly unchanged, except Gemma-2 2B ARC -9.6 (Table 2).

statements.correction: Section 4.4 and Fig 4: method works even with rho near 0. Appendix D: large rho run to convergence gives about 87% ASR, <0.1% factors below 0.9 (vs 3% in main setting), somewhat inferior quality.
statements.problem: Only one setting (rho=1e-3, converged) is tied to quality loss. The text shows no graded sparsity-versus-coherence dependence; Section 4.4 says rho is not essential. The appendix run's 87% ASR is below the main 94.3.
